title: Government Debt
scope: Public debt trajectories in rich nations and the real limits on government spending, including Modern Monetary Theory.

overview.summary: How much danger rising public debt poses to rich countries, what really limits government borrowing, and whether and how to bring debt down.
overview.scope_covered: The public debt of rich democracies, above all the United States but also Japan, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Germany and Canada: what limits their borrowing, from interest costs and inflation to investor confidence, and the main answers, including Modern Monetary Theory.
overview.scope_excluded: Debt crises in developing countries and IMF lending to them, household and corporate debt, and the mechanics of the US debt ceiling. Taxing extreme wealth and the future of money and crypto have their own pages.
overview.why_now: On September 23, 2026, the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note closed at 5.11 percent, its highest since 2007, as inflation from an oil shock and expectations of more Federal Reserve rate rises pushed up what Washington pays to borrow.

stats.label: US federal debt held by the public, share of GDP
stats.note: Debt held by the public is about one year of US output; under current law, CBO projects 120 percent of GDP by 2036 and, in its 30-year outlook, 175 percent by 2056, past the 1946 record of 106.
stats.detail: This is what the government owes outside lenders: the Federal Reserve, foreign governments, banks, funds and individuals. It leaves out about $7.8 trillion the government owes its own trust funds, so it is smaller than the more widely quoted gross debt. By the Treasury’s Debt to the Penny series, on October 1, 2026, gross debt stood at $40.26 trillion and debt held by the public at $32.43 trillion. Economists generally treat the public measure as the better gauge of the burden. The 2056 figure is from CBO’s The Long-Term Budget Outlook Data: 2026 to 2056 (February 2026). CBO’s projections assume current law continues, so they show where debt goes without new policy, not what Congress will do. In this baseline the 2025 reconciliation act (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) added $4.7 trillion to projected deficits and higher tariffs subtracted $3.0 trillion. That tariff offset has since shrunk: after the Supreme Court ruled on February 20, 2026, that the president could not impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, CBO estimated on March 5 that ending them adds $2.0 trillion to deficits over 2026 to 2036, before counting replacement tariffs. The 1946 peak came from financing World War II; the 2025 level was reached in peacetime with low unemployment.
stats.source_label: Congressional Budget Office, The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036 (February 2026)

stats.label: Social Security benefits payable once the retirement fund runs out
stats.note: Social Security’s retirement trust fund is projected to run out in late 2032; after that, incoming payroll taxes would cover 78 percent of scheduled benefits.
stats.detail: The trust fund is a reserve built from past payroll tax surpluses. Once it is gone, the law allows only the benefits current revenue can pay, an automatic cut of about 22 percent unless Congress acts. Combined with the disability fund, depletion comes in the third quarter of 2034, when 83 percent of benefits would be payable. The 75-year shortfall is 4.42 percent of taxable payroll, about 1.5 percent of GDP, up from 3.82 percent a year earlier; the Trustees attribute most of the increase to a lower assumed fertility rate. The date matters for the debt debate because Social Security and Medicare are the largest and fastest-growing parts of federal spending. Groups that want to stabilize the debt treat depletion as a forcing deadline for a combined fix; groups that want to protect benefits point out that the gap could be closed with payroll revenue instead of benefit cuts.
stats.source_label: Social Security Board of Trustees, 2026 Annual Report, Highlights

stats.label: US net interest costs and defense spending
stats.note: CBO projects federal net interest at about $1.04 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than the $885 billion spent on defense, and about $2.1 trillion by 2036.
stats.detail: Net interest is the government’s interest payments minus its interest income. CBO projects it at 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, rising to 4.6 percent in 2036, against an average of 2.1 percent over 1976 to 2025. Measured against revenue, interest would take about 19 cents of every federal tax dollar in 2026 and about 26 cents in 2036, calculated from CBO’s revenue projections of $5,596 billion and $8,301 billion. The defense figure is discretionary defense outlays, the money Congress appropriates each year. Interest is the fastest-growing major item in CBO’s projections. These projections were made in February 2026, before the long-term yields used to refinance the debt rose above 5 percent in September 2026, so actual costs depend on where rates settle.
stats.source_label: Congressional Budget Office, The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036 (February 2026)

stats.label: Share of Japanese government bonds held by the Bank of Japan
stats.note: Japan’s central bank held 46.7 percent of Japanese government bonds at the end of June 2026, down from a peak of 53.9 percent in September 2023.
stats.detail: The Bank of Japan began buying on a large scale in 2013 under Governor Haruhiko Kuroda, when it held 11.6 percent. Its purchases are widely credited with letting Japan carry the rich world’s highest debt at near-zero interest rates for a decade, and Japan is the case every camp cites. Those who doubt debt limits note that a government owing about twice its GDP has faced no default scare, partly because the debt is held overwhelmingly at home: overseas investors held about 8 percent of these bonds in mid-2026. Those who worry about debt note that the arrangement depended on near-zero rates, and that as the Bank shrinks its holdings and inflation returns, yields have risen: Japan’s 10-year yield went from 2.11 percent in early January 2026 to 3.09 percent on October 1, 2026, its highest since August 1996, by Japan’s Ministry of Finance figures. Including short-term treasury bills, the Bank’s share was 41.2 percent. The shares are at market value, so falling bond prices also lower them.
stats.source_label: Bank of Japan, Flow of Funds for the Second Quarter of 2026, Chart 6-2

stats.label: General government gross debt in major rich economies, 2025
stats.note: On a common IMF measure, Japan’s government owes about twice its GDP; Italy, the US, France and Canada owe more than a year of output, and Germany less than two-thirds.
stats.detail: These figures cover all levels of government, including states, localities and social security funds, so the US number is higher than CBO’s federal-only measure. The IMF projects the paths diverging through 2031: US debt rising to 142.1 percent of GDP, France’s to 120.7 and Germany’s to 73.7 after its 2025 borrowing reform, while Japan’s falls to 192.8 and Italy’s to 136.1 as inflation and growth raise nominal GDP faster than debt. Gross debt overstates the burden for governments that hold large financial assets. On the IMF’s net measure, which subtracts them, Canada’s debt is 10.2 percent of GDP because its public pension plans hold large reserves, Japan’s is 136.5 and the US figure 96.7. Japan’s figures changed basis in this edition, so they are not comparable with older IMF figures that put its debt well above 230 percent. Euro area members borrow in a currency their own governments do not issue, which many economists, including those who otherwise doubt debt limits, treat as a sharper constraint than the same ratio carries for the US, Japan or the UK.

stats.label: Rise in the 30-year UK gilt yield, September 2022
stats.note: After the UK’s unfunded tax-cut plan of September 23, 2022, the 30-year gilt yield rose 160 basis points in a few days, and the Bank of England stepped in to buy bonds.
stats.detail: A rise of 160 basis points is 1.6 percentage points. The episode is the closest recent case of a rich country with its own currency facing a disorderly bond market. Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng’s “growth plan” cut taxes without an independent forecast of its cost. The Bank of England reported two daily rises in the 30-year yield of more than 35 basis points, when the largest daily rise since 2000 had been 29, and found that pension funds using liability-driven investment strategies faced collateral calls that forced them to sell gilts into a falling market. On September 28 the Bank announced temporary purchases of up to £5 billion a day of long-dated gilts, and the yield fell by more than 100 basis points that day. The tax cuts were largely reversed, and Prime Minister Liz Truss resigned in October. The lessons are contested: those who stress debt limits see a market enforcing discipline on a currency issuer; others stress that UK debt was not unusually high, that the trigger was a credibility shock and a pension-fund plumbing problem, and that the central bank calmed the market within days.
stats.source_label: Bank of England, letter from Jon Cunliffe to the Treasury Committee on the LDI intervention (October 5, 2022)

stats.label: US 10-year Treasury yield
stats.note: The 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.19 percent at the start of 2026 to 5.29 percent on September 30, 2026, above its 2006 and 2007 peaks.
stats.detail: The 10-year yield is the rate investors demand to lend to the US government for a decade, and it anchors mortgage and corporate borrowing costs. By the Treasury’s daily series it last closed this high in 2002. The 30-year yield closed at 5.63 percent on October 2, 2026. Why yields rose is itself part of the debate. Those worried about the debt read part of the rise as investors demanding more to hold a growing supply of long-term bonds, a “term premium.” Those who reject that reading, such as Paul Krugman writing in August 2026, point to market measures showing little fear of default or of deliberate inflation.
stats.source_label: US Treasury, Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates

stats.label: US federal budget deficit, share of GDP
stats.note: CBO projects a 2026 federal deficit of $1.9 trillion, 5.8 percent of GDP, against a 50-year average of 3.8; the primary deficit, which leaves out interest, is 2.6 percent.
stats.detail: Deficits this large have historically come in wars and recessions; the 2026 deficit came with low unemployment. In CBO’s projections the primary deficit, spending on programs minus revenue, shrinks a little over the decade while interest grows, so a growing share of each year’s borrowing goes to pay interest. CBO projects revenue at 17.5 percent of GDP in 2026, slightly above its 50-year average of 17.3 percent, and outlays at 23.3 percent, above their average of 21.2. Each side reads that comparison its own way: one as evidence that spending is the problem, the other as evidence that revenue has not kept pace with an aging population’s commitments. Since the projection, CBO’s monthly review put the deficit near $2 trillion through the first 11 months of fiscal 2026, as reported by Fox Business. The IMF, using a general government measure that includes the states, put the 2025 US deficit at 6.8 percent of GDP.
stats.source_label: Congressional Budget Office, The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036 (February 2026)

stats.label: Public debt when recent rich-country debt crises struck
stats.note: The UK’s fiscal watchdog notes that debt crises struck Ireland at about 90 percent of GDP and Greece at about 150 percent, while Japan has had none above 200 percent.
stats.detail: The comparison is the core evidence that no single debt ratio marks a danger line. The Office for Budget Responsibility uses it to argue that what matters is a country’s circumstances: whether it borrows in its own currency, who holds its debt, how fast debt is rising, and whether investors trust the policy framework. Greece and Ireland were euro members, unable to devalue or to have their own central bank buy their bonds, until the European Central Bank’s 2012 pledge to do “whatever it takes” changed that. Ireland’s debt also jumped because its government guaranteed the banks’ liabilities. Those who worry about the US trajectory reply that the absence of a fixed line cuts both ways: crises arrive when confidence breaks, and confidence is hard to predict.
stats.source_label: Office for Budget Responsibility, Fiscal risks and sustainability (July 2026)

stats.label: Average interest rate on US marketable Treasury debt
stats.note: The average rate the US government pays on its marketable debt rose from a low of 1.42 percent in January 2022 to 3.48 percent in August 2026.
stats.detail: This is the blended rate on everything the Treasury has outstanding, from four-week bills to 30-year bonds, so it moves slowly: each month only maturing debt and new borrowing are priced at current market rates. That lag is why interest costs keep rising for years after market rates jump. In August 2026 bills averaged 3.79 percent and notes 3.35 percent, while new 10-year notes were selling near 5 percent, so the average would keep climbing as long as market rates held there. It was then still below its 2007 level, when debt was a much smaller share of the economy. The IMF’s April 2026 Fiscal Monitor flagged a related risk: the United States has leaned more on short-term borrowing in the decade to 2026, which keeps costs down when short rates are low but means more of the debt reprices quickly when rates rise.
stats.source_label: US Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service, Average Interest Rates on US Treasury Securities

stats.label: Global public debt, share of world GDP
stats.note: Government debt worldwide equaled about 94 percent of world GDP in 2025, and the IMF projects it to pass 100 percent in 2029.
stats.detail: In its April 2026 Fiscal Monitor the IMF expects the 100 percent mark one year earlier than it did in April 2025, and says the increase “largely reflects the increase in debt in the world’s two largest economies, China and the United States.” Its “debt-at-risk” measure, the level global debt would reach in a bad scenario (the 95th percentile of projections), stands at 117.2 percent of GDP for 2028. It describes the gap between interest rates and growth rates as still favorable on average, but says “its margin is narrow given countries’ relatively high interest burdens.” Advanced economies as a group carried gross debt of 108.0 percent of GDP in 2025; excluding the United States the figure was 95.3 percent and is projected to edge down. The 2020 jump reflects pandemic spending and the collapse in output; debt fell back as economies and prices recovered, then resumed rising.

stats.label: Economists on a core claim attributed to Modern Monetary Theory
stats.note: Of 38 prominent US economists polled in 2019, none agreed that countries borrowing in their own currency need not worry about deficits; MMT economists say that claim is not theirs.
stats.detail: The panel was asked about two statements. The first, counted here, read: “Countries that borrow in their own currency should not worry about government deficits because they can always create money to finance their debt.” The second read: “Countries that borrow in their own currency can finance as much real government spending as they want by creating money”; on it, 24 strongly disagreed, 11 disagreed, 3 had no opinion and none agreed. The panel spans the political spectrum and includes economists who favor more public spending. Modern Monetary Theory economists replied that neither statement describes their view: they hold that deficits do matter, through inflation, and that real resources, not money, limit what a government can buy. L. Randall Wray called the survey “polling and trolling” (New Economic Perspectives, 2019). The disagreement is partly about what the theory says, not only whether it is right.
stats.source_label: Clark Center, University of Chicago Booth School of Business, Economic Experts Panel, “Modern Monetary Theory”

stats.label: Americans calling the federal deficit a very big problem
stats.note: In April 2026, 64 percent of US adults called the deficit a very big problem, and Democrats, far less worried than Republicans in 2024, had become slightly more so.
stats.detail: Pew asked 5,103 adults how big a problem each of several issues is. The 64 percent was up from 57 percent in February 2025 and ranked behind health care affordability (73 percent) and inflation (66 percent). Under President Biden, Republicans were roughly twice as likely as Democrats to call the deficit a very big problem; by April 2026, under President Trump, the gap had closed and reversed. Analysts on every side cite the pattern. Deficit hawks read it as broad, bipartisan anxiety they can build on; those who think debt worries are overstated read it as evidence that concern tracks partisanship more than the numbers. The question measures concern, not willingness to accept any particular tax increase or spending cut.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, “Americans See Health Care Costs, Inflation as Big Problems Facing the Nation” (May 2026)

stats.label: Growth in high-debt rich countries, corrected estimate
stats.note: A 2010 study found rich countries with debt above 90 percent of GDP averaged slightly negative growth; a 2013 replication that fixed its errors put the average at 2.2 percent.
stats.detail: The figures are average annual real GDP growth in 20 advanced economies from 1946 to 2009; the original paper reported minus 0.1 percent. Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff’s paper “Growth in a Time of Debt” was cited by policymakers in the United States and Europe during the austerity debates of the early 2010s as evidence of a 90 percent danger threshold. Thomas Herndon, a graduate student, with Michael Ash and Robert Pollin, found a spreadsheet error, the exclusion of some available data and an unusual weighting method. Reinhart and Rogoff acknowledged the spreadsheet error but maintained that the corrected data still show slower growth at high debt, and the corrected figures do show high-debt countries growing more slowly than lower-debt ones. The open question, still argued, is direction: whether high debt slows growth, or slow growth produces high debt.
stats.source_label: Herndon, Ash & Pollin, “Does High Public Debt Consistently Stifle Economic Growth?” PERI, UMass Amherst (2013)

stats.label: US consumer price inflation at its 2022 peak
stats.note: US consumer prices rose 9.1 percent in the 12 months to June 2022, the largest increase since November 1981.
stats.detail: The inflation of 2021 to 2023 followed several trillion dollars of pandemic relief borrowing, including the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan of March 2021, alongside pandemic supply disruptions and the energy shock after Russia invaded Ukraine. How much of it came from fiscal policy is disputed, and the answer matters to every camp: those who stress debt limits read it as proof that heavy borrowing eventually shows up in prices, while Modern Monetary Theory economists say it confirms that inflation, not debt, is the real constraint, and attribute much of it to supply shocks. Inflation also cut the debt ratio for a time, because it raised nominal GDP faster than the debt. Inflation was elevated again in 2026: consumer prices rose 3.4 percent in the 12 months to August 2026 amid the oil shock tied to the war with Iran, as Al Jazeera reported.
stats.source_label: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index news release (July 13, 2022)

stats.label: UK tightening needed to keep debt from rising for 50 years
stats.note: The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that holding UK debt at 95 percent of GDP through 2075-76 would take a permanent tightening of 3.8 percent of GDP from 2031-32.
stats.detail: The improvement is in the primary balance and comes on top of what the government already plans. In the OBR’s long-term projections a primary deficit returns in the 2030s and reaches about 7 percent of GDP by 2075-76, driven by state pension and health spending as the population ages; with interest costs rising to 12 percent of GDP, net debt starts rising from 2032-33 and is on “a clearly unsustainable upward trajectory by the late 2040s.” The 3.8 percent is about a third larger than the tightening the government planned, as of July 2026, for the following five years and roughly equal to all onshore corporation tax receipts. Across the OBR’s scenarios the required adjustment ranges from 1.1 percent of GDP to above 8 percent. The OBR stresses that these are not forecasts, since governments would act before such paths materialized; they measure the size of the choices ahead.
stats.source_label: Office for Budget Responsibility, Fiscal risks and sustainability (July 2026)

stats.label: US government credit rating, Moody’s
stats.note: In May 2025 Moody’s cut the US rating from Aaa to Aa1, leaving the United States without a top grade from any of the three major agencies.
stats.detail: Standard & Poor’s downgraded the United States in 2011 and Fitch in 2023; Moody’s, which had rated it Aaa since 1917, was the last. Moody’s cited the rise over more than a decade in government debt and interest payment ratios to levels well above those of similarly rated countries. Ratings carry less weight for the United States than for most borrowers, because Treasury bonds are the world’s main safe asset and US debt is in dollars. In the debate they serve as a marker: those worried about the debt cite them as outside judgment that the trajectory has worsened, while those who doubt the danger note that US yields fell, not rose, in the weeks after the 2011 downgrade.
stats.source_label: Moody’s Ratings, 2025 United States Sovereign Rating Action

questions.text: Can a rich country that borrows in its own currency face a debt crisis?
questions.why: History offers no agreed danger line, and the clearest recent debt crises struck euro members that could not print their own money, which leaves open what a crisis would look like for a country that can.
questions.detail:
Those who take the risk seriously say a crisis for a currency issuer would not look like Greece’s. It would look like Britain’s gilt market in 2022, where an unfunded tax-cut plan forced the central bank to step in within days, or like a slow squeeze in which investors demand ever higher yields to hold a growing pile of long-term debt. A government can always print money to avoid default, they say, but doing so on a large scale trades a debt crisis for an inflation or currency crisis, and waiting until the market forces action means adjusting under the worst conditions.

Those who doubt the danger reply that a government owing money in a currency it issues cannot be forced into default, and that its central bank can always act as buyer of last resort, as the Bank of England did in 2022 and the Bank of Japan has done for a decade. Paul Krugman, writing in August 2026, says he has found no historical example of a Greek-style crisis in a country borrowing in its own currency. The real costs of high debt, on this view, are gradual: higher interest bills and perhaps some crowding out of private investment, which call for steady management rather than emergency austerity.

questions.text: Should debt be stabilized mainly by cutting spending or by raising taxes?
questions.why: Either path, or any mix, can close the gap. The choice turns on how large a government people want, who should bear the cost, and disputed evidence on which approach harms growth less.
questions.detail:
Those who favor spending cuts measure the problem against the country’s own history, in which revenue sits near its usual share of the economy while spending, above all on Social Security, Medicare and interest, grows faster than output. To them the fix belongs where the growth is.

Those who favor more revenue measure it against other rich democracies, most of which collect considerably more tax as a share of GDP than the United States and use it to pay for pensions and health care. To them the largest programs are commitments to retirees that most voters of every party want kept, and revenue from high earners and corporations can close much of the gap.

Each side also cites evidence that its path does less harm to growth, and that evidence is itself disputed. Most fiscal plans mix the two; the fight is over the proportions and over who bears them.

questions.text: Will interest rates on government debt stay below economic growth rates?
questions.why: When the rate a government pays is below the economy’s growth rate, debt can shrink relative to GDP even with modest deficits; when it is above, debt compounds. Rates have jumped since 2022, and no one can forecast the gap.
questions.detail:
Those who expect rates to stay below growth cite Olivier Blanchard’s 2019 presidential address to the American Economic Association, which found that safe interest rates below growth rates have been “more the historical norm than the exception” in the United States. The forces that held rates down, such as aging populations, high saving in Asia and strong global demand for safe dollar assets, have not gone away, and on this reading the jump since 2022 is cyclical. They note that as of 2026 the average rate on US debt remained below nominal growth.

Those who expect a lasting change argue that the era of near-zero rates was the exception, created by the financial crisis and central bank bond buying, and that heavy government borrowing worldwide, the end of central bank purchases, higher defense and energy spending, and persistent inflation will keep real rates higher. If long-term yields stay at their 2026 levels, the average rate on the debt will keep rising for years as old low-rate bonds mature, and the room that low rates once gave governments will shrink.

questions.text: Is inflation, rather than debt, the real limit on what a government can spend?
questions.why: Modern Monetary Theory holds that a government issuing its own currency cannot be forced to default, so inflation is its true limit. Most economists accept the premise but not the conclusion.
questions.detail:
On the Modern Monetary Theory side, economists such as Stephanie Kelton and L. Randall Wray argue that a currency issuer can always pay bills in its own currency, so the question is only whether the economy has the workers, materials and capacity to supply what the government buys without driving up prices. Interest rates, on this view, are set by the central bank rather than by the market, and taxes are the tool for cooling demand when needed. Policy should target full employment and stable prices directly.

Most economists, including many who favor more public spending, argue that debt constrains policy through channels inflation alone does not capture. Interest costs must be paid and grow with the debt, which crowds out other spending or requires higher taxes. A central bank that must hold rates down or buy bonds to keep its government funded gives up its independence to fight inflation, a situation economists call fiscal dominance. And once investors doubt a government’s commitment to stable money, inflation can arrive faster than taxes can be raised to stop it.

questions.text: Should promised retirement and health benefits be trimmed to stabilize the debt?
questions.why: Social Security and Medicare are the largest drivers of projected US spending growth, so any long-run plan must say whether their gap is closed with benefit changes, new revenue or both, a choice that divides generations as well as parties.
questions.detail:
Those who favor benefit changes argue that the programs were designed for a younger population, that benefits for future retirees are scheduled to grow faster than prices and that Medicare costs per person outgrow wages, and that closing the gap entirely with payroll taxes would mean a large tax increase on younger workers to fund older and, on average, wealthier households. Gradual changes now, such as raising the retirement age for people still decades from it, slowing benefit growth for higher earners, or competition in Medicare, would protect the most vulnerable and avoid an abrupt across-the-board cut when the trust fund runs dry.

Those who would keep scheduled benefits argue that they are earned through a lifetime of payroll taxes, that most retirees depend on Social Security for most of their income, and that raising the retirement age falls hardest on people in physical jobs with shorter life expectancies. The shortfall can be closed with revenue, for instance by applying the payroll tax to earnings above the current cap. A rich and aging society, they argue, should expect to spend more on its elderly and pay for it, rather than treat that spending as a debt problem.

questions.text: Does cutting deficits hurt the economy more than it helps?
questions.why: The answer depends on conditions: how much slack the economy has, whether the central bank can offset, whether cuts fall on spending or taxes, and whether investors were worried in the first place.
questions.detail:
The European austerity of 2010 to 2013 produced evidence for both sides. Those who warn against cuts cite Olivier Blanchard and Daniel Leigh’s 2013 IMF study, which found that forecasters had badly underestimated how much fiscal tightening would shrink European economies early in the crisis, implying that fiscal multipliers were much larger than assumed. When cuts shrink GDP, the debt ratio can rise rather than fall, as it did in several euro countries. On this view cutting deficits makes sense only at full employment, with a central bank that has room to offset.

Those who favor consolidation cite research by Alberto Alesina, Carlo Favero and Francesco Giavazzi finding that well-designed, spending-based consolidations have often been followed by mild slowdowns or even growth, as lower borrowing reduced interest rates and raised business confidence, with Canada in the 1990s and Ireland and Denmark in the 1980s as examples. Tax-based consolidations, in their findings, did far more damage to output.

questions.text: Should governments borrow to invest in infrastructure, defense and energy while debt is high?
questions.why: Public investment can raise future output and repay part of its cost, but estimates of its returns vary widely, and critics say the “investment” label gets stretched to cover everyday spending.
questions.detail:
Europe has made the choice concrete. In March 2025 Germany amended its constitution to exempt defense spending above 1 percent of GDP from its debt brake and to create a €500 billion infrastructure fund outside it, as the European Commission has described. Those who favor borrowing for investment argue that households and firms finance long-lived assets with debt, and a government should too: debt that builds roads, power grids, research capacity or military deterrence leaves future taxpayers assets as well as liabilities. Underinvestment has its own costs, from failing infrastructure to lost competitiveness and security, and fiscal rules that treat all borrowing alike push governments to cut investment first because it is easiest to delay.

Those who resist new borrowing argue that the line between investment and consumption is easily gamed, that the returns politicians promise often fail to materialize, and that a government already carrying high debt and rising interest costs should fund new priorities by cutting lower-value spending or raising taxes. Exemptions for favored categories, on this view, erode the credibility of fiscal rules and add to debt that future taxpayers must service whatever the money bought.

questions.text: Should central banks stand behind government bond markets?
questions.why: Central banks bought government bonds on a vast scale after 2008 and in 2020, and stepped into specific crises. Whether such support should be routine, and whether it costs them their independence, is disputed.
questions.detail:
Supporters of a backstop argue that the market for government debt is the foundation of the financial system, that self-fulfilling panics can push a solvent government into crisis, and that a central bank willing to act as buyer of last resort prevents that, as the European Central Bank showed when it calmed the euro crisis in 2012. Modern Monetary Theory economists go further, arguing that the central bank and the treasury are in practice one government sector whose coordination is normal.

Opponents argue that a central bank that routinely finances its government loses the ability to fight inflation, because raising rates would raise the government’s own costs, and that investors who expect a rescue stop disciplining governments. They point to the European Union’s treaty ban on central bank financing of governments: ECB President Christine Lagarde called a French presidential candidate’s 2026 proposal to cancel or freeze the French debt held by the ECB a “pure violation” of that treaty, as the Associated Press reported. With inflation above target in 2026, they also see pressure on central banks to keep government borrowing cheap as a live danger.

positions.name: Stabilize the debt soon with cuts and tax increases
positions.steelman: We are borrowing heavily at full employment and in peacetime. Fix it now, gradually and on both sides of the ledger, or be forced to fix it later in a crisis.
positions.detail:
In 2026 interest costs more than the defense budget and is on course to double by 2036, and every dollar of it is a dollar not spent on schools, troops or tax relief. No one can name the day lenders will balk, but the warning signs of 2026 are plain: long-term yields above 5 percent, a downgrade from every major rating agency, and a Treasury buying back its own bonds to steady the market. We are not predicting a default. The danger is a slow squeeze of interest costs punctuated by sudden market stress, and the low rates that rescued the warnings of the 2010s are no guarantee they will again.

The gap is too large for any single tool. Cutting only discretionary spending cannot close it, cutting only Social Security and Medicare would break promises voters will not let break, and raising only taxes would take rates that slow growth. A durable fix needs both, agreed across parties so it survives the next election. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, when gross debt passed $40 trillion in August 2026, called for no new borrowing, a deficit target of 3 percent of GDP and a bipartisan commission to repair the Social Security and Medicare trust funds; Ray Dalio’s plan reaches the same 3 percent through cuts, revenue and the lower interest rates that credible restraint would earn. And the case against austerity applies in a slump. Deficit reduction does the least harm with low unemployment and inflation above target, the conditions of 2026.
positions.proponents: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget; Maya MacGuineas; Ray Dalio

positions.name: Cut spending and grow the economy instead of raising taxes
positions.steelman: Revenue is at its historical norm and spending is not. Restrain entitlements and outgrow the debt rather than tax the economy that has to carry it.
positions.detail:
In 2026 federal revenue is at or above its 50-year average share of the economy, while spending is about two points of GDP above its own and climbing, driven by entitlement programs that grow automatically and by the interest their deficits generate. Raising taxes treats the symptom and weakens the cure: taxes on work, saving and investment shrink the economy whose growth is the least painful way to bring the debt ratio down, and in budget deals new revenue gets spent while promised cuts evaporate. In the late 1990s federal spending fell as a share of GDP and strong growth produced surpluses. So slow the growth of Social Security and Medicare for future retirees, cap and cut lower-value programs, root out waste and improper payments, and pair restraint with deregulation, cheaper energy and pro-investment tax policy.

We are told the debt came from tax cuts, including the 2025 reconciliation act. But revenue has returned to its norm even after them, so the long-run gap is on the spending side, and extending lower rates prevented a tax increase that would have slowed growth. We differ on how far growth can carry us: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says “we can grow our way out of that,” while Cato’s Romina Boccia warns that “economic growth won’t get us out of the spending-driven debt crisis” without entitlement reform. Some of us favor a balanced budget amendment, others a commission modeled on the military base-closing process.
positions.proponents: Cato Institute; Romina Boccia; Ryan Bourne; Scott Bessent

positions.name: Put investment and social programs ahead of debt reduction
positions.steelman: The debt needs steady attention, not panic. Cutting the programs that build the future does more harm than the debt, and the fair fix is revenue from those who gained most.
positions.detail:
Treating the debt as an emergency has done more damage than the debt itself. The warnings of imminent crisis around 2010 were wrong, and the austerity they justified slowed the recovery for years. The real costs of debt are higher interest bills and, at full employment, some pressure on private investment. Those are reasons to manage it steadily, not to cut Social Security, Medicare, or the investment in infrastructure, research, child care and the energy transition that makes a country more productive and its debt easier to carry. Much of the recent rise in debt comes from tax cuts that went mostly to the wealthy, so the fair and effective fix is to raise revenue from top earners and corporations.

We are told the cheap-money world this case rested on has ended. Higher rates are a real cost, as Paul Krugman acknowledges, but they are not a crisis: the 2026 rise in yields comes largely from an oil-shock inflation and a tightening central bank, and higher interest bills strengthen the case for revenue, not for cuts. We differ on how much deficit reduction to accept and when. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities favors trimming deficits gradually through progressive taxes, the Groundwork Collaborative stresses that domestic discretionary spending is already historically low, and in Europe the same view backs looser fiscal rules for investment and Mario Draghi’s 2024 call for large-scale, partly joint EU investment.
positions.proponents: Roosevelt Institute; Paul Krugman; Center on Budget and Policy Priorities; Groundwork Collaborative

positions.name: Target full employment and stable prices, not a debt ratio
positions.steelman: A government that issues its own currency cannot run out of money, only out of workers and resources. Judge its budget by jobs and inflation, not by a debt ratio.
positions.detail:
The US government spends dollars into existence. Its bonds are an interest-bearing alternative to holding dollars, and the rate they pay is ultimately a policy choice of the central bank. A deficit is the counterpart of the private sector’s savings, not a sign of failure, and a budget that balances while millions are out of work is the real waste. What a government can exhaust is workers, materials, energy and productive capacity; spend past them and prices rise. That limit is serious, so fiscal policy should be judged by employment, inflation and what it builds. When inflation threatens, target the bottleneck or use taxes to withdraw spending power. A job guarantee would give a standing buffer that grows in slumps and shrinks in booms. No country borrowing only in its own floating currency has been forced into involuntary default on that debt, and central banks bought trillions of dollars of government bonds after 2008 and in 2020 without the runaway inflation critics predicted.

We are told the 2021 to 2023 inflation proved us wrong. We always said inflation is the binding constraint; pandemic spending was designed without regard to it, and the lesson is to manage real resources better, not to target debt. Warren Mosler adds that higher rates are themselves a central bank choice that pays income to the private sector and can feed inflation. Our framework does not apply to euro members, which borrow in a currency they do not issue. Nor is it the plan, floated in France’s 2026 presidential race, to cancel or freeze the French bonds the European Central Bank owns, which rests on a separate claim.
positions.proponents: Stephanie Kelton; L. Randall Wray; Levy Economics Institute; Warren Mosler

crux.lead: Is rising debt in rich countries a sudden danger or a slow cost they can manage?
crux.lead_highlight: a sudden danger or a slow cost
crux.subtitle: Most agree that a government borrowing in its own currency cannot be forced to default. The split is over whether its growing debt could still force a sudden, painful adjustment through interest costs, inflation or lost investor confidence, or stay gradual enough to manage over decades.
crux.empirical: Part of it can be measured: whether interest rates stay below growth as debt rises, whether investors demand a growing premium to hold long-term government bonds, how strongly deficits at full employment feed inflation, and how costly cutting deficits is in different conditions. More years of bond-market data and long-run budget projections will narrow it, though no data can say when confidence would break.
crux.values: The rest is a choice. Even with the risk known, people differ on how much present benefit, in public investment, retirement and health care, or lower taxes, is worth trading for a smaller chance of a future crisis; on whether the cost should fall on today’s taxpayers, today’s retirees or tomorrow’s workers; on how large a government they want; and on whether a debt ratio should be a goal of policy at all.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a classical treasury building with a triangular pediment and four plain columns standing on a low rise as the dominant focal mass; a tall stack of rolled bond certificates, each tied with a ribbon, in front of the building's lower right corner and overlapping its steps; a medium open ledger book lying at the lower left; a small arched stone bridge far behind on the rise; one road curving unbroken across the whole frame from the lower left, past the building steps and over the small bridge as the connective element; the ground is the gentle curve of a low rise.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #b48f2c, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: dollar signs, euro signs, currency symbols, numbers, banknotes, coins, piggy banks, hands, arrows going up or down, graphs, charts, debt clocks, clocks, chains, shackles, balls and chains, cliffs, cracks, bombs, scales of justice, a printing press, flags, a row of identical buildings.
